title: Gerunds and Infinitives
summary: Choosing between the -ing form and the to-infinitive after verbs, objects, prepositions and adjectives.

sections.heading: Verbs That Take the -ing Form
sections.body:
A large group of verbs is followed directly by the **gerund**, the `-ing` form working as a noun. The core members are `enjoy`, `avoid`, `consider`, `suggest`, `deny`, `risk`, `mind`, `practise` and `involve`, along with `admit`, `postpone`, `imagine` and `finish`.

The pattern is fixed: nothing comes between the verb and the `-ing` form, and no `to` appears. `suggest` is the one most often mishandled, because its alternative is not an infinitive but a clause: `suggest doing` or `suggest that we do`, never `suggest to do`.

Arabic expresses both the verbal noun and the subordinate clause in ways that translate most naturally into English as `to` plus a verb, which is why `enjoy to read` and `avoid to speak` are such persistent slips. The remedy is to store these verbs as a closed list rather than to reason from meaning.

examples.right: The board is considering relocating the research centre.
examples.wrong: The board is considering to relocate the research centre.
examples.note: `consider` is followed by the -ing form only.

examples.right: She suggested postponing the vote until March.
examples.wrong: She suggested to postpone the vote until March.
examples.note: Use `suggest doing` or `suggest that we postpone`.

examples.right: The role involves working with three separate teams.
examples.wrong: The role involves to work with three separate teams.
examples.note: `involve` names an activity, so the -ing form follows.

sections.heading: Verbs That Take the To-Infinitive
sections.body:
A second group takes `to` plus the base verb: `decide`, `hope`, `manage`, `refuse`, `afford`, `offer`, `agree`, `fail`, together with `promise`, `arrange`, `intend`, `pretend` and `tend`.

Most of these describe an intention, a decision or an outcome that lies ahead of the first verb in time, which is a useful memory aid: one decides now in order to act later. The negative is formed with `not to`, placed before `to`, as in `decided not to appeal`.

examples.right: The council decided to fund the cycle lanes for a further year.
examples.wrong: The council decided funding the cycle lanes for a further year.
examples.note: `decide` belongs to the to-infinitive group.

examples.right: Few households can afford to heat every room in winter.
examples.wrong: Few households can afford heating every room in winter.
examples.note: `afford` takes the to-infinitive.

examples.right: The authors failed to acknowledge two earlier studies.
examples.wrong: The authors failed acknowledging two earlier studies.
examples.note: `fail to do` is the only pattern available.

sections.heading: Both Forms, Different Meanings
sections.body:
A small set accepts either pattern, and the choice changes the meaning rather than the style. With `stop`, `remember`, `forget` and `regret`, the `-ing` form points backwards to something already done, while the to-infinitive points forwards to a duty or a purpose.

`try doing` means testing a method to see whether it helps; `try to do` means attempting something difficult. `go on doing` continues the same activity, whereas `go on to do` moves to the next one. `mean doing` states a consequence that follows; `mean to do` states an intention.

`need` is the odd member: `need doing` carries a passive sense and is equivalent to `need to be done`.

examples.right: He stopped checking his phone and finished the chapter.
examples.note: `stop doing`: the activity comes to an end.

examples.right: On the way north we stopped to refuel.
examples.note: `stop to do`: a pause for a purpose.

examples.right: I regret telling her before the results were confirmed.
examples.note: `regret doing` looks back at a past action.

examples.right: The roof needs repairing before the winter.
examples.note: `need doing` is passive in sense: it needs to be repaired.

sections.heading: Verb Plus Object Plus Infinitive
sections.body:
Many verbs take an object and then a to-infinitive, the object naming the person who performs the second action: `want`, `expect`, `advise`, `persuade`, `encourage`, `allow`, `enable`, `remind`, `warn` and `force`.

Three verbs break the pattern and take a **bare infinitive** after the object: `make`, `let`, and `have` in the sense of arranging for something to be done. `help` permits both, with or without `to`, and neither version is more correct than the other.

One detail is easy to miss: in the passive, `make` recovers its `to`, so `The staff made him wait` becomes `He was made to wait`.

examples.right: The tutor encouraged her to submit the paper early.
examples.wrong: The tutor encouraged her submitting the paper early.
examples.note: verb + object + to-infinitive.

examples.right: The new policy lets residents park free at weekends.
examples.wrong: The new policy lets residents to park free at weekends.
examples.note: `let` takes a bare infinitive.

examples.right: The delay made passengers miss their connections.
examples.wrong: The delay made passengers to miss their connections.
examples.note: `make` plus object plus bare infinitive in the active voice.

examples.right: Passengers were made to wait on the platform for an hour.
examples.note: In the passive, `make` is followed by `to`.

sections.heading: After a Preposition, Always -ing
sections.body:
Every preposition is followed by the `-ing` form and never by an infinitive: `without asking`, `before leaving`, `by reducing`, `instead of complaining`, `capable of measuring`.

The difficulty is that `to` is sometimes a preposition rather than the marker of an infinitive. In `look forward to`, `be used to`, `get used to`, `object to`, `be committed to`, `in addition to` and `when it comes to`, `to` is a preposition and the `-ing` form must follow it.

Compare that with `used to` plus a base verb, an entirely different structure describing a discontinued past habit. `He used to cycle` means he no longer does; `He is used to cycling` means it now feels normal to him. The test is whether a form of `be` or `get` stands in front of `used`.

examples.right: We look forward to receiving your confirmation.
examples.wrong: We look forward to receive your confirmation.
examples.note: `to` here is a preposition, so the -ing form follows.

examples.right: She is used to working under tight deadlines.
examples.wrong: She is used to work under tight deadlines.
examples.note: `be used to` describes a familiar situation.

examples.right: The library used to open on Sundays.
examples.note: `used to` plus base verb: a past habit that has stopped.

examples.right: Emissions fell by replacing coal with gas.
examples.wrong: Emissions fell by replace coal with gas.
examples.note: After `by`, as after any preposition, the -ing form.

sections.heading: The -ing Subject and Adjective Patterns
sections.body:
Because the `-ing` form behaves as a noun, it can head the subject of a sentence and takes a singular verb: `Commuting by train has become more expensive`. A base verb can never do this.

After an adjective the two patterns both occur but are not interchangeable. A to-infinitive follows the adjective directly in `difficult to measure`, `easy to explain`, `likely to rise`, `ready to publish` and `willing to pay`. When a preposition intervenes, the `-ing` form is required: `capable of measuring`, `interested in studying`, `responsible for monitoring`, `good at explaining`, `afraid of failing`.

examples.right: Commuting by train has become more expensive than driving.
examples.wrong: Commute by train has become more expensive than drive.
examples.note: The -ing form, not the base verb, can head a subject.

examples.right: The sensors are capable of detecting a change of one degree.
examples.wrong: The sensors are capable of detect a change of one degree.
examples.note: `of` is a preposition, so the -ing form follows.

examples.right: The results were difficult to interpret.
examples.wrong: The results were difficult of interpreting.
examples.note: `difficult` takes a to-infinitive with no preposition.

slips: `suggest to do` is not English. Write `suggest doing` or `suggest that we do`.
`look forward to` ends in a preposition, so it takes the -ing form: `look forward to meeting you`, never `to meet`.
`He used to cycle` is a past habit; `He is used to cycling` is present familiarity. Check whether a form of `be` or `get` precedes `used`.
`make` and `let` take a bare infinitive in the active (`made him wait`), but passive `make` restores the `to`: `was made to wait`.
`stop to do` is a pause for a purpose; `stop doing` ends the activity. Decide which the sentence means before choosing.
After any preposition use the -ing form: `interested in studying`, not `interested in to study`.

questions.prompt: The planning committee suggested ___ the consultation by a further month.
questions.explain: `suggest` belongs to the -ing group. `to extend` is the commonest error, because the only clause alternative is `suggested that the consultation be extended`, not an infinitive.

questions.prompt: The department looks forward to ___ from applicants before the end of the month.
questions.explain: In `look forward to`, `to` is a preposition rather than an infinitive marker, so the -ing form is required.

questions.prompt: She first outlined the sampling method and then went on ___ the results in detail.
questions.explain: `go on to do` marks a move to the next stage, which `first ... and then` signals. `go on doing` would mean she continued outlining the method.

questions.prompt: The new regulations will make manufacturers ___ their emissions every quarter.
questions.explain: Active `make` takes an object and a bare infinitive. `to report` would only be correct in the passive, as in `manufacturers will be made to report`.

questions.prompt: We regret ___ you that the funding application has not been successful.
questions.explain: `regret to do` introduces bad news at the moment of delivering it; `regret informing` would look back on the act of telling as a past mistake.

questions.prompt: Having spent a decade in Oslo, he is used to ___ in near-darkness through December.
questions.explain: `be used to` means accustomed to, and its `to` is a preposition, so an -ing form follows. `used to work` would instead describe a habit he has abandoned.

questions.prompt: The university could not afford ___ the whole laboratory in a single year.
questions.explain: `afford` takes the to-infinitive; there is no `afford doing` pattern in standard English.

questions.prompt: The contractor denied ___ any of the safety notices sent to the site office.
questions.explain: `deny` is followed by the -ing form or by a that-clause. Unlike `refuse`, which takes an infinitive, `deny` reports a past act, and the gerund carries that backward reference.

questions.prompt: The instrument is capable of ___ concentrations far below the legal limit.
questions.explain: `capable of` ends in a preposition, so the -ing form is required; the infinitive appears only after adjectives used without a preposition, such as `able to analyse`.

questions.prompt: ___ the findings without checking the raw data would be premature.
questions.explain: A subject must be nominal, and the -ing form supplies that. A base verb cannot head a subject, and `To publishing` combines an infinitive marker with an -ing form.

questions.prompt: Before the tram line opened, most residents ___ into the centre every morning.
questions.hint: drive (a past habit that has stopped)
questions.explain: `used to` plus a base verb states a discontinued habit, and `would drive` is equally correct for a repeated past action of this kind. The similar-looking `were used to driving` would say only that driving felt normal to them.

questions.prompt: Please remember ___ the data appendix when you send the final version.
questions.explain: `remember to do` concerns a task not yet carried out. `remember including` would mean recalling that the appendix had already been added.
